<explanation>
Below is our recommended approach to drawing a detailed, accurate system design diagram for AzurLaneAutoScript – a complex, modular automation bot for Azur Lane with an integrated GUI.

1. Identify the project’s essence:
   • It is not a “typical” client–server full stack app; instead, it is an automation bot built to control a mobile game (Azur Lane) 24/7.
   • The README explains multiple core features like “出击”, “收获”, “每日”, and “大世界” tasks plus advanced scheduling and mood control. This tells you that the system must manage concurrent task execution, timed scheduling, and state management for gameplay.
   • The wide-ranging file tree shows a highly modular codebase that separates concerns among tasks, device control, campaign logic, configuration, GUI interfaces, deployment scripts, and even “submodules” bridging with external tools.

2. Analyze the file structure for architectural insights:
   • Directories like “module/” contain many purpose-built submodules (campaign, combat, commission, device, config, map, etc.) that encapsulate the game automation logic.
   • “deploy/” and “bin/” folders contain deployment and binary assets (e.g., Android APKs, device-specific tools, Docker-related files). This shows that the bot runs on different platforms and communicates with mobile devices via ADB, scrcpy, and other device methods.
   • “webapp/” suggests there is also a web-based or electron-based GUI component.
   • “dev_tools/” and “submodule/” provide utilities and bridges (e.g., AlasFpyBridge, AlasMaaBridge) that help extend functionality or interface with related projects.
   • The presence of multiple internationalized asset directories (assets\cn, assets\en, etc.) along with i18n JSON files in “module/config/i18n” underscores support for multilingual interfaces.

3. Define the main system components for your diagram:
   a. GUI/Front End:
      - Draw the GUI layer using components from the “webapp” folder (Electron-based and Vue components) along with Python GUI components (PyWebIO likely used in the main script or module/gui).
      - Represent this as the user’s interaction entry point.

   b. Scheduler / Task Management:
      - Include a “Scheduler” component that receives tasks (for “科研”, “出击”, “收获”, etc.) and dispatches them based on timing and current game state.
      - In the diagram, show arrows from the Scheduler to various Task Modules.

   c. Core Bot Modules:
      - Represent the core “module/” folder as a collection of submodules. Group them logically (for example, Campaign, Combat, Guild, Equipment, Event, Daily, MapDetection, etc.).
      - Indicate that each module serves a specific automation function. Use separate boxes (or grouped boxes) with clearly labeled names.

   d. Device Interface and Communication:
      - Include a “Device Management” or “Interface Layer” (covered in module/device along with methods for adb, scrcpy, etc.) showing how the system commands and receives feedback from emulators and real devices.
      - Connect this component to the core modules to represent that various tasks use these interfaces to interact with the game.

   e. Configuration & I18n:
      - Diagram a “Configuration” component that consolidates configuration handling (module/config, i18n files) and is used by other modules.
      - Indicate that configuration information flows to the Scheduler and core task modules, affecting behavior (for example, mood thresholds and scheduling delays).

   f. Deployment & External Utilities:
      - Although not directly affecting runtime behavior, include a side box for “Deployment Tools” (deploy/, dev_tools/) that manages packaging (like Docker, Windows-specific scripts, etc.) and submodule integration.
      - Optionally show external integration points such as Discord notifications and remote control.

4. Representing relationships and interactions:
   • Use directional arrows showing that:
       – User interactions via the GUI trigger the Scheduler.
       – Scheduler dispatches tasks to the appropriate core modules (each task with distinct logic for different game features).
       – Core modules use the Device Interface to command device interactions (and then receive status feedback that may go back to the Scheduler).
       – Configuration is read by both the Scheduler and modules to manage parameters like timing delays and international settings.
       – External Deployment components (Docker, Windows utilities, etc.) provide additional infrastructure support but are isolated from core task execution.
   • Color-code different component types (e.g., blue for GUI, green for core modules, orange for device interface, purple for configuration, gray for deployment/utilities).

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram to this project:
   • Because this project is very modular with many functionally distinct components, focus on capturing the primary “flows” – start with user initiation from the GUI, go through the scheduler, branch into task-specific modules, and then to device control.
   • For each module (like “campaign”, “os_handler”, “combat”, “map_detection”), include a note that they individually encapsulate distinct automated game interactions.
   • Emphasize in the diagram that the system has a centralized scheduling/orchestration logic that drives nearly all operations seamlessly (“无缝收菜”).
   • Don’t try to capture every one of the hundreds of files; instead, depict high-level boundaries and interactions.
   • Use labels and grouping: each component box should be clearly labeled, and interactions should be marked with directional arrows. Optionally add annotations about critical technologies (e.g., Python scripting, ADB via module/device/method, Docker deployment, PyWebIO for GUI).

6. Final notes on diagram elements:
   • Include clear labels for each component (e.g., “User GUI (Electron/Vue)”, “Scheduler/Task Manager”, “Campaign Module”, “Device Interface (ADB/Scrcpy)”, “Configuration & i18n”, “Deployment Utilities”).
   • Directional arrows indicate data flow and control – from GUI to Scheduler, from Scheduler to modules, and from modules to the device interface.
   • Use different colors or shapes (e.g., rounded rectangles for services, squares for external tools) to visually differentiate layers.
   • Ensure the diagram is detailed enough to capture all essential components and their interactions, yet not so cluttered as to lose clarity. It is acceptable to provide a hierarchical diagram which shows a “big picture” first with links to more detailed sub-diagrams for complex modules.

By following these guidelines, you will produce a comprehensive and tailored system design diagram that clearly delineates the modular architecture of AzurLaneAutoScript – from user interactions, through the scheduling engine and diverse automation modules, to the low-level device interface and deployment mechanisms.
</explanation>
